passage: Neelam, don't laugh, okay? You know Rawat sir, the new history teacher? He says 'Let's question the source' before every lesson, and now I say it too. I said it at dinner! Papa asked what I meant and I just repeated sir's line. I've started reading everything he mentions. Three books this month, me, Gargi, who used to sleep in history! But yesterday sir said village farming never changed for centuries, and I wrote it down like scripture. Then you showed me that chapter saying it did. I felt weird. Like, can sir be wrong? Of course he can. It just never crossed my mind.

qa.q: How many books has Gargi read this month?
qa.a: Three books this month.

qa.q: What was Gargi feeling when Neelam showed her the chapter?
qa.a: She felt weird and unsettled, because she had never imagined Rawat sir could be wrong and had treated his words like scripture.

qa.q: What could help Gargi at this stage of admiring her mentor?
qa.a: She could keep the reading habit sir sparked while checking his claims against other sources, and even ask him about the chapter, so admiration feeds her own judgement.

qa.q: How might Neelam see Gargi's new way of talking?
qa.a: Neelam may find it funny and a bit worrying, glad Gargi loves history now but noticing she repeats sir's lines instead of her own thoughts.

grounding: A teenage girl describes copying her male teacher's phrases and treating his views as truth, until a wrong claim shows his limits.

passage: I'm Sahil, Dolma's classmate, and I've watched her change since Mr Chettri took over debate club. She used to argue with everyone. Now she starts sentences with 'As Mr Chettri says.' When Karma questioned one of his rules in practice, Dolma snapped, 'He's been doing this for twenty years.' She carries his marked-up notes around like certificates. Her speeches are sharper, honestly, and she won the district round. But at lunch I asked what she thought about school uniforms, and she said, 'I'll ask him.' I don't know if she noticed how that sounded. I did.

qa.q: What did Dolma win?
qa.a: She won the district round.

qa.q: What might Dolma's snapping at Karma show about how she sees Mr Chettri?
qa.a: It suggests she admires him so much that questioning him feels like an attack, as if his view must be the truth.

qa.q: What could Mr Chettri do to support Dolma's growth at this stage?
qa.a: He could invite disagreement in practice and ask Dolma for her own opinion before sharing his, so her admiration turns into independent thinking.

qa.q: How does Sahil feel about the change in Dolma?
qa.a: He sees real gains, like sharper speeches and a win, but is uneasy 🤔 that she no longer seems to trust her own opinions.

grounding: A classmate observes a teenage girl adopting her male coach's phrases and opinions, growing in skill while losing her own judgement.

passage:
Dear Priti didi,
You asked about school. Jatin sir is honestly the best teacher I have ever had. He says "Data first, drama later," and now I say it too, even to Mummy about the dishes! Papa says his beti has turned into a professor. He says debate teams win on structure, so I rewrote all my notes his way. When my friend suggested a different opening for our debate, I told her sir wouldn't like it, and we dropped it.
I've started reading every article he mentions. I stay up late to finish them. Sometimes I wonder what I think before he says anything. But mostly I just want to be like him.
Write back soon!
Mehak

qa.q: What phrase does Jatin sir say that Mehak now repeats?
qa.a: "Data first, drama later."

qa.q: What does Mehak's letter show she feels about Jatin sir?
qa.a: Mehak feels deep admiration and excitement; she copies his phrases and wants to be like him.

qa.q: What could Mehak try at this stage to keep her own judgement?
qa.a: Before asking what sir would think, write down her own view first, and give her friend's idea a fair try.

qa.q: What might Mehak's friend experience when her opening is dropped?
qa.a: The friend may feel dismissed or hurt that sir's imagined opinion counted more than her idea.

grounding: Shows a student copying her mentor's phrases and treating his views as truth, with hints of losing her own judgement.

passage:
So you know Anirban sir, the one who runs the astronomy club? Honestly, he's changed how I see everything. He says "Look up before you look it up," and I've written it on my notebook cover. My brother laughs because I say it at dinner now.
Last week our group argued about whether to observe from the roof or the field. I said the field, because sir once said open ground is best. I didn't even think about the power lines by the field. Sir didn't correct me, he was busy. We lost an hour.
Still, I'd do anything he suggests. I'm Gurleen, by the way, the girl who always sits in the front row.

qa.q: What has Gurleen written on her notebook cover?
qa.a: "Look up before you look it up."

qa.q: What does Gurleen feel about Anirban sir?
qa.a: Gurleen feels strong admiration and eagerness to please, so much that his old comment outweighed her own thinking.

qa.q: What went wrong in the roof-or-field choice, and what could fix it next time?
qa.a: Gurleen used sir's old line instead of checking the actual field; next time she could check the conditions herself first.

qa.q: How might Gurleen's group see her lean on sir's words?
qa.a: They may feel frustrated at losing an hour because a remembered quote was treated as the final answer.

grounding: Shows a student copying her mentor's phrases and treating his views as truth, which hides her own judgement.

passage:
Week one: Harleen came out of Sumit sir's history class glowing. "He says history is just people making choices," she told Kamal at the gate, eyes bright.
Week three: Harleen used the line in every essay. When Kamal said a book claimed something different, she snapped, "Sumit sir says otherwise." Kamal shrugged and walked on.
Week five: Sumit sir returned her essay with one note: "Whose argument is this? I want yours." Harleen read it twice on the bus, frowning, then went to the library and reread the book Kamal had mentioned, pencil in hand, making her own notes.

qa.q: What note did Sumit sir write on Harleen's essay?
qa.a: "Whose argument is this? I want yours."

qa.q: How was Harleen feeling in week five when she read the note twice?
qa.a: She seemed confused and a little stung, perhaps unsettled that the teacher she admired wanted her own thinking, not his.

qa.q: What turning point does Sumit sir's note offer?
qa.a: It pushes Harleen to test ideas herself, like rereading the book Kamal mentioned, instead of repeating sir.

qa.q: What is it like for Kamal when Harleen snaps at him in week three?
qa.a: Kamal may feel brushed off and a bit hurt that a book he found counted for nothing against sir's word.

grounding: Shows a student's admiration for her mentor turning into copying his words and dismissing other views, until he pushes back.

passage: Uday, you think your Avni Dadi always had her own opinions? At fifteen I worshipped Mr Bose, our physics teacher. He said "Elementary!" whenever something was obvious, so I said "Elementary!" at dinner until my brothers begged me to stop. He thought poetry was a waste of time, so I stopped reading poetry, though I had loved it since I was small. If he said a film was foolish, it was foolish. My notebooks were full of his phrases. That admiration made me study harder than ever, it's true. But one day he wrote a wrong answer on the board, and I defended it to my friend Kamala for twenty minutes before I checked the book. My own head had gone quiet, beta. I had handed it over to him.

qa.q: What did Mr Bose say whenever something was obvious?
qa.a: He said "Elementary!"

qa.q: How did the young Avni feel about Mr Bose?
qa.a: She felt a deep, eager admiration, almost worship, so strong that she echoed his phrases and gave up the poetry she loved.

qa.q: When the young Avni checked the book and found Mr Bose's answer was wrong, what could she take from that turning point?
qa.a: She could keep admiring him while using her own judgement again, checking facts herself and returning to the poetry she loved.

qa.q: What might Kamala have felt during those twenty minutes of argument?
qa.a: Kamala may have felt frustrated and puzzled that her friend defended a wrong answer so fiercely just because Mr Bose had said it.

grounding: Shows a student idealising a teacher, copying his phrases and taking his opinions as truth, which fuels effort but hides his limits and her own judgement.
